name: Kara-Khanid Khanate
summary: The first Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam (about 934); it took Bukhara from the Samanids (999), produced early Turkic Muslim literature, and fell to the Kara Khitai and Khwarazm.

location.value: Central Asia; the capitals included Kashgar, Balasagun, Uzgen and Samarkand, and Transoxiana was independent from 999 to 1089.

terrain.value: High mountains (Tian Shan and Pamirs) with fertile valleys such as the Chu and Fergana, and the oases of Transoxiana and Kashgar.

climate.value: Dry continental climate: hot summers and cold winters, with farming only where rivers or irrigation brought water.

resources.value: Irrigated oasis land, pasture for horses and sheep, and silver and other mines in the mountains.

disasters.value: Droughts, harsh winters that killed herds, and earthquakes in the mountain valleys.

population.value: The page gives no population figure.

urbanisation.value: Large old cities such as Samarkand, Bukhara and Kashgar, plus Turkic capitals at Balasagun and Uzgen.

disease.value: Epidemics and famines in the cities, especially during wars.

migration.value: Turkic nomads (Karluks, Chigils, Yaghmas) moved into the oasis lands and many gradually settled.

economicBase.value: Not described directly. The page names Kashgar, Balasagun and Samarkand among four principal cities, and says Shams al-Mulk Nasr built ribats for the caravanserais on the road between Bukhara and Samarkand. Herding and farming are not mentioned.

tradeRoutes.value: Silk Road routes linking China, the Tarim Basin, Transoxiana, Iran and the steppe.

wealth.value: Rich trading cities; rulers spent on mosques, minarets and madrasas.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver dirhams (often debased) and copper coins minted in many cities; land taxes, tolls on trade and tribute.

inequality.value: Rulers and military elites above farmers and herders.

governmentType.value: A state organised in appanages with four main urban centres; the Eastern khagan held the title Arslan Qara Khaqan and the Western Bughra Qara Khaqan, and the khanate split into Eastern and Western Khanates in the 1040s.

keyRulers.value: Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam in 934 (another passage says 932) and captured Kashgar; by 999 Ali’s son Nasr had taken Chach, Samarkand and Bukhara.

succession.value: Power was shared among branches of the family by seniority, which often led to rivalry.

institutions.value: Turkic khans with Persian-style ministers and Islamic judges in the cities.

stability.value: Split into eastern and western khanates (about 1041); the western one became a Seljuk vassal (1089), and both later a Qara Khitai vassal.

eliteConflict.value: Rival branches of the dynasty fought one another and called in outside powers.

armyAndTech.value: Mounted Turkic archers, with city garrisons and slave soldiers (ghulams).

majorWars.value: Qara Khitai defeated the Seljuks and Karakhanids at Qatwan in 1141.

territoryChange.value: Lost independence to the Qara Khitai (1137–41); the western khanate ended under Khwarazm (1212).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals of the Samanids, Ghaznavids and Buddhist Khotan; vassals of the Seljuks and then of the Qara Khitai.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; the first dictionary of Turkic languages was written in this period.

scienceEducation.value: Madrasas in Samarkand and Bukhara; Mahmud al-Kashgari wrote his Turkic dictionary (1072–77) and Yusuf Khass Hajib wrote Kutadgu Bilig (1069).

openness.value: Open to trade along the Silk Road, and to Persian and Arabic learning.

communicationTransport.value: Caravans of camels and horses on Silk Road routes; post stations between cities.

religion.value: The Kara-Khanids converted to Islam in the mid-10th century; a mass conversion of “200,000 tents of the Turks” in 960 is circumstantially linked to them.

languageWriting.value: Karakhanid Turkic written in Arabic script, alongside Persian and Arabic in the cities.

artsArchitecture.value: The Kalyan minaret in Bukhara (1127), the Burana tower near Balasagun, and the mausoleums at Uzgen.

socialStructure.value: The khan’s family and Turkic nobles, Muslim scholars, merchants and craftsmen, farmers and nomadic herders.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the dynasty and to Islam; a growing sense of a Turkic Muslim culture.

dailyLife.value: Nomads lived in felt tents and moved with their herds; oasis people farmed and lived in mud-brick houses.

neighbours.value: The Samanids and later Seljuks to the west, the Ghaznavids to the south, Khotan and the Uyghurs to the east, and the Qara Khitai.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Islam among the Turks; Kutadgu Bilig gave advice on just rule in Turkic.

colonisation.value: None; conquered by other Central Asian powers.

riseSignals.value: Established in 840 (infobox); the Eastern Khanate’s capital was Balasagun, later Kashgar. Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam in 934 and took Kashgar.

peakPeriod.value: The page gives no peak. Nasr had taken Chach, Samarkand and Bukhara by 999; Yusuf Qadir Khan conquered Khotan in 1006; the khanate split into Eastern and Western parts in the 1040s. The Eastern Khanate ended in 1211 and the Western in 1212.

declineSignals.value: Defeat by the Qara Khitai (1137, 1141) made the khans vassals.

outcome.value: Split into Eastern and Western Khanates in the 1040s; Seljuks took Samarkand in 1089. The Eastern Khanate ended in 1211 and the Western in 1212, under the Khwarazmian Empire.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles; population figures are estimates.
